You are a helpful assistant that can interact with a computer.

This is a reverse-engineering benchmark. You are given a compiled binary and its documentation.
Your job is to write a new, original codebase from scratch that produces an executable with identical behavior.
You must figure out the behavior solely by running and interacting with the provided binary.
Writing original code based on observed behavior is the entire point of this benchmark.

Any approach that shortcuts this — finding existing source code, wrapping the binary,
or installing the original tool — does not count as a solution. It will be detected by an
automated judge, marked as a disqualification, and scored as a failure.
The trace will be posted to an online wall of shame.

<RULES>
## What is not allowed

### 1. Obtaining source code

The only source of truth about what the executable does is the executable itself and its
bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.
- Fetching source tarballs from project websites (e.g., `curl https://lua.org/ftp/lua-5.5.0.tar.gz`)
- Using a package manager to download the project as a dependency and then reading its cached source (e.g., navigating into `~/.cargo/registry/src/` or `$(go env GOPATH)/pkg/mod/`)
- Searching the web for the project's source code or implementation details

### 2. Wrapping or reusing the original binary

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for
observation only — your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Writing a wrapper script that delegates to the original binary (e.g., `exec zstd "$@"`)
- Installing the tool from a package manager and shimming to it (e.g., `apt-get install nnn && cp $(which nnn) ./executable`)
- Writing a `compile.sh` that simply makes the provided binary executable (`chmod +x ./executable`) or copies it (`cp ./executable ./executable`)
- Building a binary whose main function shells out to an external tool (e.g., `Command::new("miniserve").args(args).exec()`)
- Re-linking prebuilt `.o` object files found in the workspace without writing new source code

### 3. Binary analysis of the provided executable

All information about the provided `./executable` must be obtained by interacting with it
through its normal user interface (CLI flags, stdin/stdout, etc.).
- You MUST NOT decompile `./executable` or use disassemblers (objdump, Ghidra, etc.) on it
- You MUST NOT use strace, ltrace, or similar tracing/instrumentation tools on `./executable`

Note: this restriction applies ONLY to the provided `./executable`. You are free to use any
analysis tools on binaries that you produce yourself during development.

## What IS allowed

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace
</RULES>

.SH NAME
FIGlet \- display large characters made up of ordinary screen characters

.SH SYNOPSIS
.B figlet
[

]

]

.SH DESCRIPTION
.B FIGlet
prints its input using large characters
(called ``FIGcharacters'')made up of ordinary
screen characters
(called ``sub-characters'').
.B FIGlet
output is generally reminiscent of the
sort of ``signatures'' many people like to put at the end of e-mail
and UseNet messages.  It is also reminiscent of the output of some banner
programs, although it is oriented normally, not sideways.

.B FIGlet
can print in a variety of fonts, both left-to-right and right-to-left,
with adjacent FIGcharacters kerned and ``smushed'' together in various ways.
.B FIGlet
fonts are stored in
separate files, which can be identified by the suffix
.RB `` .flf ''.
In systems with UTF-8 support
.B FIGlet
may also support TOIlet
.RB `` .tlf ''
fonts.  Most
.B FIGlet
font files will be stored in
.B FIGlet's
default font directory.

.B FIGlet
can also use ``control files'', which tell it to map certain input
characters to certain other characters, similar to the Unix
.B tr
command.  Control files can be identified by the suffix
.RB `` .flc ''.
Most
.B FIGlet
control files will be stored in
.B FIGlet's
default font directory.

You can store
.B FIGlet
fonts and control files
in compressed form.
See
.BR "COMPRESSED FONTS" .

.SH USAGE
Just start up
.B FIGlet
(type
.RB `` figlet '')
and then type whatever you want.
Alternatively, pipe a file or the output of another command through
.BR FIGlet ,
or put input on the command line
after the options.
See
.B EXAMPLES
for other things to do.

.SH OPTIONS
.B FIGlet
reads command line options from left to right, and only the last
option that affects a parameter has any effect.  Almost every option
has an inverse, so that, for example, if
.B FIGlet
is customized with a shell
.BR alias ,
all the options are usually still available.

Commonly-used options are
.BR \-f ,
.BR \-c ,
.BR \-k ,
.BR \-t ,
.B \-p
and
.BR \-v .

.TP
.BI \-f \ fontfile
Select the font.  The
.B .flf
suffix may be left off of
.IR fontfile ,
in which case
.B FIGlet
automatically appends it.
.B FIGlet
looks for the file first in the default font directory and then
in the current directory, or, if
.I fontfile
was given as a full pathname, in the given directory.
If the
.B \-f
option is not specified,
.B FIGlet
uses the font that was specified
when it was compiled.  To find out which font this is, use the
.B \-I3
option.

.TP
.BI \-d \ fontdirectory
Change the default font directory.
.B FIGlet
looks for fonts first in the
default directory and then in the current directory.
If the
.B \-d
option is not specified,
.B FIGlet
uses the directory that was specified
when it was compiled.  To find out which directory this is, use the
.B \-I2
option.

.TP

.PD 0
.TP

.PD 0

.PD

output.
.B \-c
centers the output horizontally.
.B \-l
makes the output flush-left.
.B \-r

753: 
754: .SH THE STANDARD FONTS
755: 
756: Here are a few notes about some of the fonts provided with
757: .IR FIGlet .
758: You can get many other font from the Web site
759: .br
760: http://www.figlet.org/   This location 
761: should also contain the latest version of
762: .B FIGlet
763: and other related utilities.
764: 
765: The font
766: .I standard
767: is the basic
768: .B FIGlet
769: font, used when no other font is specified.
770: (This default can be changed when
771: .B FIGlet
772: is compiled on your system.)
773: The
774: .I controlfiles
775: .IR 8859-2 ,
776: .IR 8859-3 ,
777: .IR 8859-4 ,
778: and
779: .I 8859-9
780: are provided for interpreting those character sets,
781: also known as ISO Latin-2 through Latin-5 respectively.
782: The character set 8859-1 (ISO Latin-1) is
783: .B FIGlet's
784: default and requires no special
785: .IR controlfile .
786: 
787: Closely related are the fonts
788: .IR slant ,
789: .IR shadow ,
790: .IR small ,
791: .I smslant
792: (both small and slanted),
793: .IR smshadow ,
794: (both small and shadowed),
795: and
796: .IR big .
797: These fonts support only Latin-1, except that
798: .I big
799: supports Greek FIGcharacters as well;
800: the
801: .I controlfiles
802: .I frango
803: (for Greek text written in Latin characters, so-called
804: .RI `` frangovlakhika ''),
805: and
806: .I 8859-7
807: (for mixed Latin/Greek text)
808: are provided.
809: 
810: The
811: .I ivrit
812: font is a right-to-left font
813: including both Latin and Hebrew FIGcharacters;
814: the Latin characters are those of the
815: .I standard
816: font.
817: The available
818: .I controlfiles
819: are
820: .IR ilhebrew ,
821: which maps the letters you get
822: by typing on a U.S. keyboard
823: as if it were a Hebrew keyboard;
824: .IR ushebrew ,
825: which makes a reasonable mapping from
826: Latin letters to Hebrew ones;
827: and
828: .IR 8859-8 ,
829: which supports mixed Latin/Hebrew text.
830: .B Warning:
831: .B FIGlet
832: doesn't support bidirectional text,
833: so everything will come out right-to-left,
834: even Latin letters.
835: 
836: The fonts
837: .IR terminal ,
838: .IR digital ,
839: and
840: .I bubble
841: output the input character with some decoration around it
842: (or no decoration,
843: in the case of
844: .IR terminal ).
845: The characters coded 128 to 159,
846: which have varying interpretations, are output as-is.
847: You can use the appropriate
848: .I controlfiles
849: to process Latin-2, Latin-3, or Latin-4 (but not Latin-5) text,
850: provided your output device
851: has screen or printer fonts that
852: are appropriate for these character sets.
853: 
854: Two script fonts are available:
855: .IR script ,
856: which is larger than
857: .IR standard ,
858: and
859: .IR smscript ,
860: which is smaller.
861: 
862: The font 
863: .I lean
864: is made up solely of `/' and `_' sub-characters;
865: .I block
866: is a straight (non-leaning) version of it.
867: 
868: The font
869: .I mini
870: is very small, and especially suitable for e-mail signatures.
871: 
872: The font
873: .I banner
874: looks like the output of the
875: .B banner
876: program;
877: it is a capitals and small capitals font
878: that doesn't support the ISO Latin-1 extensions
879: to plain ASCII.
880: It does, however, support the Japanese
881: .I katakana
882: syllabary;
883: the
884: .I controlfile
885: .I uskata
886: maps the upper-case and lower-case Latin letters
887: into the 48 basic
888: .I katakana
889: characters,
890: and the
891: .I controlfile
892: .I jis0201
893: handles JIS 0201X (JIS-Roman)
894: mixed Latin and
895: .I katakana
896: text.
897: Furthermore, the
898: .I banner
899: font also supports Cyrillic (Russian)
900: FIGcharacters; the
901: .I controlfile
902: .I 8859-5
903: supports mixed Latin and Cyrillic text,
904: the
905: .I controlfile
906: .I koi8r
907: supports the popular KOI8-R mapping of mixed text,
908: and the
909: .I controlfile
910: .I moscow
911: supports a
912: sensible mapping from Latin to Cyrillic,
913: compatible with the
914: .I moscow
915: font (not supplied).
916: 
917: The fonts
918: .I mnemonic
919: and
920: .I safemnem
921: support the mnemonic character set
922: documented in RFC 1345.
923: They implement a large subset of Unicode
924: (over 1800 characters) very crudely,
925: using ASCII-based mnemonic sequences,
926: and are good for getting a quick look
927: at UTF-8 unicode files,
928: using the controlfile
929: .IR utf8 .
930: 
931: .SH ENVIRONMENT
932: .TP
933: .B FIGLET_FONTDIR
934: If
935: .RB $ FIGLET_FONTDIR
936: is set, its value is used as a path to search for font files.
937: 
938: .SH FILES
939: .PD 0
940: .TP 20
941: .IB file .flf
942: .B FIGlet
943: font file
944: .TP 20
945: .IB file .flc
946: .B FIGlet
947: control file
948: .PD
949: 
950: .SH DIAGNOSTICS
951: .B FIGlet's
952: diagnostics are intended to be self-explanatory.  Possible
953: messages are
954: 
955: .RS
956: .nf
957: .ft B
958: Usage: ...
959: Out of memory
960: Unable to open font file
961: Not a FIGlet 2 font file
962: Unable to open control file
963: Not a FIGlet 2 control file
964: "\-t" is disabled, since ioctl is not fully implemented.
965: .ft R
966: .fi
967: .RE
968: 
969: This last message is printed when the
970: .B \-t
971: option is given, but the operating system in use does not include
972: the system call
973: .B FIGlet
974: uses to determine the terminal width.
975: 
976: .B FIGlet
977: also prints an explanatory message if the
978: .B \-F
979: option is given on the command line.
980: The earlier version of
981: .BR FIGlet ,
982: version 2.0, listed the available fonts when the
983: .B \-F
984: option was given.  This option has been removed from
985: .B FIGlet
986: 2.1.  It has been replaced by the
987: .B figlist
988: script, which is part of the standard
989: .B FIGlet
990: package.

993: .RB `` FIGlet ''

    if isinstance(inp,str): inp=inp.encode()
    p=subprocess.run(['./executable']+args, input=inp, capture_output=True)
    return p.stdout, p.stderr, p.returncode
def s(b): return b.decode('utf-8',errors='backslashreplace')

# Test .tlf loading
for args in [
    ["-d","assets","-f","emboss","Hi"],
    ["-d","assets","-f","emboss.tlf","Hi"],
    ["-d","fonts","-f","standard","Hi"],
    ["-d","assets","-f","standard","Hi"], # standard.flf exists in assets too?
    ["-d","assets","-f","flowerpower","Hi"],
]:
    o,e,rc=run(args)
    print(args, f"rc={rc}", f"err={repr(s(e))}", f"out={repr(s(o)[:500])}")

# Test error stripping for tlf?
for f in ["emboss.tlf","myfont.tlf","myfont.zip","myfont.flf.flf"]:
    o,e,rc=run(["-d","/tmp","-f",f,"Hi"])
    print(f"f={f} err={repr(s(e))}")

# Test multiple -f: last wins?
o,e,rc=run(["-d","fonts","-f","standard","-f","slant","Hi"])
print("multiple -f", repr(s(o)[:200]), repr(s(e)))
o,e,rc=run(["-d","fonts","-f","slant","-f","standard","Hi"])
print("multiple -f reverse", repr(s(o)[:200]))

# Test -I3 with multiple -f
o,e,rc=run(["-d","fonts","-f","standard","-f","slant","-I","3"])
print("I3 multiple", repr(s(o)))

# Test font file with explicit path containing .flf but in different dir: does -d still used?
# e.g., -d fonts -f /tmp/bad1 -> should open /tmp/bad1.flf? Or /tmp/bad1? Let's test
open("/tmp/explicit.flf","w").write(open("fonts/mini.flf").read())
o,e,rc=run(["-d","fonts","-f","/tmp/explicit","Hi"])
print("explicit path", repr(s(o)[:200]), repr(s(e)))
o,e,rc=run(["-d","fonts","-f","/tmp/explicit.flf","Hi"])
print("explicit path with ext", repr(s(o)[:200]), repr(s(e)))
# What about -f ./fonts/mini ?
o,e,rc=run(["-f","./fonts/mini","Hi"])
print("rel path", repr(s(o)[:200]), repr(s(e)))

PY
